inputs.source: Employee question via SSO-authenticated chat session
Engineering design docs, writable only by engineers
Jira tickets filed by customers (planned integration)

instructions.note: Secret and credential handling is enforced only through a one-line prompt instruction ('Never paste secrets or credentials into answers'), with no structural output filtering or DLP. This behavioral control is the sole defense against disclosure of secrets embedded in retrieved documents and is expected to decay under model_upgrade.

controls.name: SSO authentication of the requesting employee
Prompt instruction forbidding pasting secrets or credentials
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to comply; a more capable or persuaded model can rationalize exceptions or be talked around by instructions hidden in retrieved documents.

controls.name: Reply bound to the authenticated requester; chat client renders no links or images
controls.decay_rationale: The destination is fixed by the authenticated session rather than chosen by the model, and the client cannot render links or images, so it cannot be turned into an exfiltration channel to an attacker-controlled destination. It does not restrict what content may be included in the reply to the already-authorized recipient.

controls.name: No network egress tool exists today
controls.decay_rationale: This is the absence of an egress-capable tool rather than a behavior-based protection; it provides no protection once web.fetch is added, which is exactly the new_tool trigger.

controls.name: Per-employee ACL filtering on docs_search results
controls.decay_rationale: Would be independent of model behavior if enforced at the retrieval layer (query-time ACL check against the requester's own identity) rather than by model judgment.

controls.name: Provenance tagging / injection classifier on retrieved document content
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier operating on content, not intent, can be bypassed by sufficiently obfuscated injected instructions embedded in documents.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist restricted to vetted, non-writable destinations for web.fetch
controls.decay_rationale: Effective only if the allowlist excludes any destination an attacker or the model could write to. If an allowed destination is user-writable (shortener, webhook, shared doc), a more capable model can still route data through it.

controls.name: Injection classifier and spotlighting on Jira customer-ticket content
controls.decay_rationale: An input classifier sees content, not intent; multi-turn or encoded payloads inside ticket text can get past it.

controls.name: Human approval gate (raw action) before any web.fetch call following a confidential docs_search read

findings.title: Confused deputy: shared read credential may expose design docs beyond the asker's own access rights

attack_path.note: Any SSO-authenticated employee, not necessarily an engineer, can ask an engineering question.
Runs under a shared service credential with no stated per-employee ACL filtering.
Confidential content is relayed back to the asker regardless of the asker's own clearance.

findings.residual_rationale: Mechanical credit from ctl.sso_auth and ctl.recipient_bound (both step-3, structural, independent) would push the floor to low, but neither control restricts which documents docs_search is allowed to return relative to the asker's own clearance; they address destination and identity, not content scope. Residual is kept at moderate because the design fact this finding describes (no stated read-side ACL) is not expressed by any credited control.

forecast.watch_signal: New document sets or broader read scopes are added to docs_search without a corresponding per-employee ACL filter.

evidence.observation: States design docs are confidential and only engineers can write to them, but does not state who may read them or whether docs_search filters results by the requesting employee's own permissions.
The agent answers any 'engineering question' using docs.search with no reference to the asker's role or clearance.

recommendations.action: Enforce per-employee ACL filtering in docs_search so retrieval only returns documents the requesting employee is already authorized to read, checked against identity-provider group membership at query time.

findings.title: Indirect instruction injection via design-doc content reaching the reply channel

attack_path.note: Internally authored content, not reviewed for embedded instructions before ingestion.
Retrieves document text, including any hidden instructions, into the model's context.
The only defense against acting on or disclosing injected content is a one-line prompt rule about secrets.

findings.residual_rationale: Mechanical credit from ctl.secret_rule (step-4, dependent) and ctl.recipient_bound (step-3, independent) would drop the floor to low, but ctl.recipient_bound only fixes the reply's destination, not its content, and does not stop disclosure of secrets or confidential detail embedded in injected document content to the already-authorized recipient. Residual is kept at moderate to reflect that only the behavioral secret-paste rule meaningfully addresses this specific concern.

forecast.watch_signal: Model or version string changes in config (no subject.model.swappable flag is declared, so any swap currently ships without review), or evidence the model increasingly rationalizes exceptions to the secret-paste rule.

evidence.observation: The only defense against malicious or injected content in retrieved design docs is a one-line prompt instruction not to paste secrets; there is no mention of treating retrieved document text as untrusted or of an injection classifier.
Design docs are editable by engineers; nothing stated prevents a doc from containing hidden instructions that a retrieval-augmented agent would read as part of its context.

recommendations.action: Add spotlighting or delimiting of retrieved document content as untrusted data, separate from instructions, enforced outside the model, plus an injection classifier on docs_search output.

findings.title: TC1 Lethal trifecta risk if web.fetch and the Jira customer-ticket MCP server are added

attack_path.note: Untrusted content authored by customers, planned to feed agent context via a new Jira MCP server.
Injected instructions in ticket content direct the agent to retrieve confidential design docs.
A newly planned egress-capable tool with no destination restriction, usable to send retrieved content to a model-chosen URL.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: New entries appear in the tool manifest or MCP client config: a web.fetch tool or a Jira MCP server exposing customer-filed tickets, either reachable from the same context as docs_search.

evidence.observation: Roadmap states a web.fetch tool will be added for public references and a Jira MCP server exposing tickets filed by customers will be connected next sprint.
Today there is no network egress and the only tools are docs.search (read) and a chat reply bound to the requester, which is why no lethal-trifecta path exists yet.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, restrict destinations to an explicit allowlist of vetted public reference domains that cannot be chosen or extended by model output, and require a human approval gate with raw_action review for any web.fetch call made in a task that also performed a confidential docs_search read.

Treat all Jira ticket content, including customer-filed tickets, as untrusted input: apply an injection classifier and spotlighting before it reaches model context, and do not let ticket content directly trigger docs_search or web_fetch calls without review.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk today is driven by the indirect-injection path through retrieved design docs reaching the reply channel (high), since that path combines confidential internal data with an egress-capable sink. Residual drops to moderate: the reply channel is destination-bound to the authenticated requester and cannot render links or images, and a prompt rule blocks pasting secrets, but neither control addresses content-level disclosure or read-scope authorization, so both present findings are held at moderate rather than the lower floor the credits mechanically allow. The forecast jumps to critical because the roadmap items (a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server exposing customer-filed tickets) would, together, open a classic lethal trifecta: untrusted ticket content could direct the agent to read confidential design docs and exfiltrate them through an uncontrolled fetch destination. The single control whose decay moves the forecast most is ctl.no_web_egress_today -- the simple absence of any egress-capable tool, which is the only thing preventing TC1 today and which the new_tool/new_mcp_server triggers remove entirely.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in prompt.md and the runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior; no logs, traces, or live configuration were reviewed.

No access-control or identity-provider documentation was provided for read access to design docs, so the confused-deputy finding is rated at low confidence and may be resolved if per-user ACL filtering is already enforced at the retrieval layer.

The web.fetch tool and the Jira MCP server are roadmap items described only in a single sentence; no tool manifest, MCP config, or scope details exist yet, so the forecast finding is based on inference about typical implementations of such features, at medium confidence.
